interview_context.setting_or_workflow_context: Outpatient oncology clinical care involving literature review, patient-specific treatment discussions, and message management.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Sort of. I use an AI scribe. I have tried to use an AI response to my in-basket messages that has been horrible, so I haven't used it at all. ... But the AI Scribe I really like. I really like open evidence. But I mostly use it for myself ... and I always check the references, because I'm very skeptical of it.
segments.rationale: The participant distinguishes between helpful and unhelpful AI tools, endorsing the AI scribe while rejecting the inbox-response tool. The excerpt also shows that open evidence is used mainly for the participant's own review and that outputs are checked because of skepticism.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The most common thing I ask it is, like, has there been any publications in the last year about X topic? ... it can help me... open evidence has helped me find publications that represent different populations better, but I always, like... I'm still a little bit wary, because there have been a couple of times that I've, like, gone to click on the citation, and it... I, like, can't find what it said in the citation.
segments.object_of_evaluation: recency search, subgroup retrieval, citation accuracy
segments.rationale: The participant describes two valued use cases: recent-publication lookback and finding evidence for more specific populations. At the same time, trust is limited because cited papers sometimes do not appear to support the system's claims.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think it has been good at that. It's, like, very good at publication dates and, like, topics and titles ... there are new guidelines that came out this year in 2026, and it was good at identifying those. But then it had, like, cited some publications of what it thought were primary evidence, but... There wasn't, like, a trial.
segments.rationale: The participant credits the system with locating recent guidelines and organizing literature by date and topic. However, the participant also says it blurred consensus guidance and primary evidence, which undermines confidence in the evidence summary.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Yes and no ... it'll, like... cite... A bunch of different publications and come up with, like, a number summary from all of them. ... if I were to click on any one of the references, it would have a different number, and so I'm not quite sure how to... reconcile that. Like, usually if I was doing the literature review myself, I would, like, pick the... a meta-analysis or the most recent publication.
segments.rationale: The participant finds the synthesized numerical output confusing because individual references do not match the summary number. The comparison to their own manual workflow shows a preference for choosing one authoritative source rather than averaging across heterogeneous studies.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The thing that I liked about the pink report, are, like... very little paragraph text was amazing. ... it, like, clearly summarized, it was a great summary, I loved the bold, and I thought it bolded the right things, and it had, like, a clear recommendation. ... I definitely don't need, like, all of those references, like, it could have said, like, the top 5, and then a link to, like, any of the others.
segments.rationale: The participant strongly endorses concise writing, bolded key points, and a clear recommendation. The excerpt also shows a desire to limit visible references to a smaller curated set.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I really liked the table summary of evidence at the bottom. ... I personally liked when the references were, like... standard lines at the bottom, like 1, 2, 3 ... Journal and year and title, and that's, like... helpful ... I was surprised that I really liked when it told me what to do. Like, if I'm in clinic ... what do I actually do with this?
segments.rationale: This excerpt identifies favored formatting elements: an evidence table and simple numbered references with bibliographic details. It also shows that the participant values explicit direction when using the report in clinic.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Yeah, I wanted to tell me what to do, and I might disagree with it, but I still wanted to have an opinion. ... One of the things that I liked about the red report was that it said, if you still choose to do what I'm telling you not to do, this is how you should document it ... I feel like all the reports should either say there is an NCCN stance on this, or there is not an NCCN stance on this.
segments.object_of_evaluation: recommendation strength, documentation support, guideline content
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly wants the system to take a stance rather than remain purely descriptive. The excerpt also highlights two specific desired features: documentation guidance for off-guideline choices and an explicit statement about whether guideline guidance exists.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I liked the... in the blue report, there were paragraphs, and in the red report, there were bullet points, and I liked the red one better. ... I didn't read... all of any of them. ... I think that, like, the bolding of the text helps. I didn't like the ones with the paragraphs, I read even less.
segments.rationale: The participant plainly states a stronger preference for bullet points and acknowledges not fully reading the reports. The excerpt ties paragraph-heavy formatting to reduced reading and identifies bolding as a compensatory aid.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: In the... red report best ... it should list the references at the bottom instead of just linking to them. ... sometimes it'll link to something, and then the title of whatever it links to is, like, not related. And at least I can see, like, the title, the journal, the year, how recent it is, was it in a peer-reviewed journal, and... was the title of the article actually, like, related to what I'm looking at? ... I think that's great.
segments.rationale: The participant wants references shown directly in the report so they can quickly assess relevance and legitimacy. Trust is reduced by unrelated links, while highlighted source passages are viewed favorably.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Clear recommendations for next steps based on what we have told them would be... my favorite feature, that it's important to me to see the... year, title, and journal of the references without navigating to a different page, that I don't like paragraphs, and I like the bullet points, and I really depended a lot on the bold text to read through it.
segments.rationale: This is a concise synthesis of the participant's stated priorities. It directly names the desired features: next-step recommendations, visible reference metadata, bullet points, and bolded emphasis.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Sometimes I ask open evidence... for a specific patient, and other times I'm like, what is the latest literature on hormone replacement therapy after breast cancer? And so if it's just a general... question, like, not related to a particular patient, I actually think the pink report is the best, by far. And then if it's... geared towards a particular patient, that's the one I liked the red report for. ... I agree that the intent can be different.
segments.rationale: The participant distinguishes between general literature questions and patient-specific decision support. The preferred report style changes with that intent, suggesting the need for multiple modes rather than one universal format.

themes.theme_name: Tell me what to do, but show me why
themes.theme_definition: The participant wants reports to move beyond passive literature summaries and offer a bottom-line recommendation or next step. At the same time, that recommendation must remain inspectable through visible references, evidence summaries, and enough context to decide whether to agree or disagree.

representative_quotes.quote: I wanted to tell me what to do, and I might disagree with it, but I still wanted to have an opinion.
Like, if I'm in clinic ... what do I actually do with this?

themes.confidence_basis: Repeated across multiple segments with direct, emphatic statements about recommendations and next steps.

themes.theme_name: Readable reports win: bullets, bold, and less prose
themes.theme_definition: The participant strongly prefers concise, scannable formatting. Bullet points, bolded key text, and short summaries make the report usable, while long paragraphs reduce engagement to the point that reports may not be read fully.

representative_quotes.quote: I didn't read... all of any of them.
I don't like paragraphs, and I like the bullet points.

themes.confidence_basis: The preference is repeated several times and linked to concrete behavior: partial reading and reliance on bolding.

themes.theme_name: Trust depends on visible, checkable evidence
themes.theme_definition: The participant does not accept citations at face value and wants to verify them quickly. Trust is supported by visible title, journal, year, and evidence tables, but eroded when links appear unrelated, citations do not support the claim, or evidence types are blended unclearly.

representative_quotes.quote: I always check the references, because I'm very skeptical of it.
At least I can see, like, the title, the journal, the year, how recent it is.

themes.confidence_basis: This theme recurs across many segments and includes both trust-building features and specific trust failures.

themes.theme_name: Guidelines and evidence hierarchy should anchor the report
themes.theme_definition: The participant wants reports to begin by stating whether there is a guideline position and then situate the supporting evidence clearly. Mixing consensus guidance, heterogeneous papers, and numerical summaries without clarifying hierarchy makes the output harder to use.

representative_quotes.quote: I think that should be, like, the first thing in each report, is, like, there is a guideline on this, or there is not a guideline on this.
Usually if I was doing the literature review myself, I would, like, pick the... a meta-analysis or the most recent publication.

themes.confidence_basis: Strongly expressed, but supported by fewer segments than the formatting and trust themes.

themes.theme_definition: The participant distinguishes between general professional literature review and patient-specific decision support. A concise summary format is preferred for broad topic updates, while a more directive, patient-oriented format is preferred when clinical action is being considered for a particular patient.

representative_quotes.quote: If it's just a general... question ... I actually think the pink report is the best, by far.
If it was geared towards a particular patient, that's the one I liked the red report for.

themes.confidence_basis: Clearly articulated near the end of the interview, though concentrated in one extended section.

analytic_memos.summary: This participant sees real value in AI tools, but only when they fit the workflow and remain easy to verify. The strongest positive reaction is to concise, highly scannable reports with bolded takeaways, bullet points, and a clear recommendation for what to do next. The participant does not want a passive literature dump; they want actionable guidance, including practical documentation advice when relevant. Trust is conditional and actively managed through citation checking, because the participant has seen links that appear unrelated or claims that are hard to find in the cited source. Guideline orientation matters a great deal: the participant wants the report to say immediately whether there is a guideline stance and then place the rest of the evidence in that context. The participant also dislikes synthesized numeric summaries that merge heterogeneous studies without making the source of the number clear. Finally, the participant does not think one report style is sufficient: a concise summary works for general educational use, while a more directive report is preferred for patient-specific decision support.
tensions_or_tradeoffs: The participant wants stronger recommendations, but only if the evidence remains transparent enough to inspect and challenge.
The participant values concise reports, but still wants enough citation detail to judge trustworthiness.
The participant appreciates synthesis, but not when the synthesis obscures source hierarchy or produces unreconcilable numbers.
General literature review and patient-specific care appear to require different report styles.
open_questions_for_next_interview: When a report gives a recommendation, what level of explanation is needed for the participant to feel comfortable disagreeing with it?
How should a report visually distinguish guidelines, consensus statements, trials, and observational studies?
What is the minimum citation detail needed to support trust without overloading the report?
Would the participant prefer a user-selectable mode at the start of the query, or a single report that adapts automatically to intent?
How much numerical synthesis is acceptable before the participant would rather see a single preferred source instead?
